column13: notes
Tolerates low light but variegation fades. Roots easily in water from a cutting.
More white in the leaf means less chlorophyll — needs brighter light than golden and grows slower.
Leaf holes appear with maturity and enough light, not with age alone. Wants something to climb.
Thinner leaves than deliciosa, dries out faster, and shows crisp edges sooner if the air is dry.
One of the few genuinely low-light-tolerant trailers. Pinch tips to stop it going bare at the top.
Variegation is unstable — cut back to a variegated node if it reverts to plain green.
Wants floor space more than height. Older plants form a visible trunk.
Stores water in rhizomes. The most common way to kill one is watering it on a schedule.
Happy pot-bound. Water far less in winter — cold wet soil is what rots them.
Same care as trifasciata. The fanned braid is done at the nursery, not by the plant.
Brown tips are usually fluoride and salts in tap water. Rainwater or distilled fixes it.
Wilts dramatically then recovers, which trains people to underwater it. Water before the droop.
New growth emerges lime green and darkens to near-black. Slower than the plain form.
Drops lower leaves when moved. Give it one spot and leave it there.
Hates change and cold draughts. Brown crispy edges are usually underwatering; dark spots are usually over.
Leaf drop after any move is normal and it grows back. Keep away from doorways.
More forgiving than a fiddle leaf and often sold as its easier replacement.
Sensitive to fluoride — brown tips are usually the tap water, not the watering.
Slow and long-lived. Wipe the leaves; dust noticeably dulls it.
Same plant as corn plant with brighter variegation and the same fluoride sensitivity.
Wants more direct sun than most houseplants. Rot from overwatering is the usual end.
Not a palm. The swollen base is a water store — treat it like a succulent.
One of the few palms that genuinely copes with low light. Prone to spider mite in dry air.
Expensive because it is slow. Very tolerant of low light and neglect once settled.
Thirsty and humidity-hungry. Brown tips are almost always dry air or fluoride.
Sold everywhere and struggles indoors — it wants swamp humidity and strong light.
Dries out fast. A pebble tray does more than misting, which is over by the time you put the bottle down.
Unforgiving about drying out — one missed week and the fronds crisp. Best in a bathroom.
Water the soil, not the central rosette — water sitting in the crown rots it.
An epiphyte. Usually mounted, and soaked rather than watered.
The furry rhizomes belong on the surface — burying them rots the plant.
Crisp edges mean tap water or dry air. Rainwater or distilled, and keep it off a radiator.
Folds its leaves up at night. Drooping in daylight is thirst or cold.
Reclassified out of Calathea but sold under the old name everywhere.
Leaves fold at dusk and open at dawn. Stops doing it when it is unhappy.
The pink is real variegation, not a dye. Needs bright light to keep it.
Same family and the same demands as Calathea — humidity and clean water.
Grown for foliage, not flowers. Never mist — wet leaves invite mildew.
Cane-type. Needs staking once it gets tall or it snaps under its own weight.
Water from the bottom. Cold water on the leaves leaves permanent pale rings.
The red part is a spathe, not a petal. Blooms for months in enough light.
Not potted in soil. Bark mix, a soak once a week, and never leave it sitting in water.
A jungle cactus, not a desert one — it wants more water than it looks like it should.
Wrinkled leaves mean thirst; soft mushy ones mean too much. Very long-lived.
Wants far more sun than it usually gets indoors. Drain sharply.
Stretching towards the window means not enough light — rosettes should stay tight.
Tolerates less light than most succulents. Small enough for a windowsill forever.
Shrivelled beads mean underwatering; mushy ones mean over. Shallow roots want a shallow pot.
Tubers along the strands can be pressed into soil to make new plants.
Leaves drop at the lightest touch. Put it somewhere it will not be brushed past.
Rotate it weekly or it leans hard towards the light. Produces pups you can separate.
Semi-succulent leaves — treat it more like a succulent than a tropical.
Striped leaves scorch in direct sun. Bright but filtered.
Flowers only when a bit pot-bound. Never cut off the bare flower spur — it reblooms from it.
A single leaf sold in a pot will usually never grow — it needs a node to become a plant.
Gets leggy in low light. Prune hard and it branches.
The larger cousin, and better suited to a bright corner than a shelf.
Colour needs strong light. Drops every leaf when moved, then regrows them.
One of the genuinely low-light plants. Pink and red cultivars need more light than green ones.
Sap is a serious irritant — the common name is a warning. Wash hands after pruning.
Leaves change shape as it matures — arrow-shaped young, lobed later.
Grows fast and goes bare at the base. Cut it back hard twice a year.
Needs strong light for the pink. Pinch tips constantly to keep it full.
Collapses theatrically when dry and recovers within hours of watering. A terrarium plant really.
Dies back and looks dead, then returns from the tubers. Let it rest rather than binning it.
Goes dormant in winter and looks dead. Keep it barely moist and it comes back.
Striped stems are the point. Spider mites love it — check the undersides.
A bog plant. It can sit in a saucer of water, which is true of almost nothing else here.
Grown from tubers, dies back every year, and that is normal rather than a failure.
Named for what it survives. Genuinely the plant for a dark hallway.
Not a real pine and not frost hardy. Drops lower branches permanently if it dries out.
The braid is done at the nursery. Yellow leaves are usually too much water.
Not bamboo. Usually grown in water — change it fortnightly and keep it off tap water.
No soil at all. Soak for 20 minutes weekly and shake it out — trapped water in the base rots it.
Distilled or rainwater only — tap water minerals kill it. Never feed it meat.
Needs a cold winter dormancy. A windowsill all year round will exhaust it.
Pitchers form only in high humidity. Distilled water, never fertiliser in the soil.
Spider mites are near-inevitable in dry indoor air. Rinse the foliage monthly.
Tougher than English ivy indoors and far less mite-prone.
Not ivy. Grows fast, roots from any cutting, and wants pinching often.
The purple fuzz needs bright light. The flowers smell unpleasant — most people cut them off.
Short-lived and leggy. Pinch constantly, and take cuttings before it gives up.
Silver markings are natural. Cut back hard in spring to stop it sprawling.
Textured leaves hold water — a pebble tray suits it better than misting.
Pinch the flower spikes the moment they appear or the leaves turn bitter.
Invasive in the ground. Keep it in a pot of its own, always.
More rosemary is killed by overwatering than by cold. Sharp drainage matters most.
Mediterranean — poor soil and full sun. Rich compost makes it floppy and flavourless.
Flavour is strongest just before it flowers.
Biennial — it bolts in its second year and that is the end of it.
Bolts fast in heat. Sow a new pot every three weeks rather than fighting it.
Cut from the outside. Shearing the whole clump to the base sets it back weeks.
Woody and short-lived. Replace every three or four years.
Does not transplant well — sow it where it will grow.
Spreads like mint. Pot it.
Wants poor, gritty, dry soil. Feeding it is how most people kill it.
Water at the base and evenly — irregular watering is what splits fruit and causes blossom end rot.
Needs warmth more than anything. Cold nights stall it completely.
Bitter fruit is usually irregular watering. Give it something to climb.
Bolts in heat. Afternoon shade buys weeks.
Cool-season. Sow in spring and again in autumn, not in midsummer.
Sweeter after a frost. Pick from the bottom up and it keeps producing.
Forked roots come from stony or freshly manured soil, not from bad seed.
Ready in a month. All leaf and no root means too much nitrogen.
Fixes its own nitrogen — do not feed it like a tomato.
Cool-season and quick. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked.
Bulb size is set by day length — pick a variety for your latitude.
One plant feeds a household. Two feeds a street.
Runners drain the parent. Cut them off unless you want more plants.
The velvet finish only holds in humid air; in dry rooms new leaves come out matte and smaller.
A sport, so it can revert to plain green or go fully white. Remove all-white leaves — they cannot feed themselves.
Self-heading, so it stays a mound rather than climbing. Wider than it is tall.
Pink is variegation, not a flower. Half-pink leaves are the target; a fully pink leaf will brown off.
New leaves unfurl burgundy and settle to dark green. Wipe the leaves — they show dust badly.
Slow, and the white sections photosynthesise nothing. Prune back to a variegated node if a plain green run takes over.
Not a monstera and not a philodendron. Fast on a pole, leggy without one.
Leaves stay small and silver-blue until it climbs; given a pole they fenestrate and change shape entirely.
Brightest in good light — in a dim corner the neon dulls to ordinary green.
The silver is a surface layer; do not scrub it. Tolerates a dim room better than most trailers.
The red holds in medium light, unlike most coloured foliage. Sulks below 15°C.
One of the genuinely low-light-tolerant plants in this list, and forgiving of a missed week.
Goes dormant rather than dying when unhappy — if it drops every leaf, keep the tuber barely moist and wait.
Small and slow. The velvet leaves mark with water spots, so water the soil and not the plant.
Textured leaves trap dust and spider mites. Check the undersides monthly.
Thirsty and fast in warmth. Outdoors in summer it doubles; indoors it slows right down.
Grown for the white veining, not flowers. Wants a chunky bark mix, not potting compost.
New leaves emerge coppery and soft, then harden. Do not touch them while they unfurl.
The largest peace lily sold. Same wilting habit as the small one, but a full-size plant droops hard enough to look dead.
Red stems, heart leaves, and far less fuss than the aroids it resembles.
Sap irritates mouth and throat — the common name is literal. Wash hands after pruning.
Slower and fussier about light than the plain form; too much feed turns the stripes green.
A dwarf, so it stays a tabletop plant. Same intolerance of being moved as the full-size tree.
Drops leaves at any change — light, draught, new pot. Leaf fall after a move is normal, not a diagnosis.
The swollen root is the point. Sold as bonsai; prune the top to keep the proportion.
Thicker leaves than benjamina and far less prone to dropping them.
Goes leggy fast in low light. Cut it back hard in spring and it branches rather than stretching.
Drops leaves in dry winter air and looks dead for a month, then re-flushes. Do not repot it in a sulk.
Wants a cool room. Above 22°C all winter it goes soft and pale.
Sold as a grafted stump. Water at the base only; the trunk rots if it sits wet.
Tubular leaves with red tips in strong sun. Green tips mean it wants more light, not more water.
Blue-grey coin leaves. Slower than common jade and even less tolerant of a wet winter.
Powder-coated leaves; handling rubs it off permanently. Drops leaves readily and each one is a new plant.
Hardy outdoors through frost. The main rosette dies after flowering — that is the plant finishing, not failing.
Re-blooms only after about six weeks of long, uninterrupted nights. A lamp in the room is enough to stop it.
Furry leaves hold water against the surface — water the soil, never overhead.
Drops plantlets from every leaf edge and they root in any nearby pot. Keep it away from other plants.
Not a cactus. The white sap burns skin and eyes — gloves, and never prune it near your face.
The orange only develops in full sun and cool nights. Same caustic sap as the rest of the genus.
The fine golden tufts are glochids and are far worse than spines — they detach on contact and are hard to remove.
Flowers in a ring around the crown if given a dry, cold winter rest with no water at all.
The coloured top is a mutant with no chlorophyll, grafted onto the green base. It lives only as long as the graft does.
Very slow. A specimen the size of a football is decades old, which is what you are paying for.
Not a desert cactus. Needs more water than it looks like, and buds drop if it is moved while setting.
A jungle cactus that grows in tree forks — it wants humidity and shade, not a windowsill bake.
Night-flowering, one night only, strongly scented. Buds form after a cool dry spell.
Faster and far more forgiving than string of pearls, and it fails the same way — from the top, in wet compost.
The dolphin shape only forms on mature growth in good light; new strands come out plain.
Forms tubers along the strands. Pin one onto compost and it roots without cutting anything.
Semi-succulent leaves — it stores water, so treat it as a succulent rather than a peperomia.
The most shade-tolerant common succulent. Tolerates a north window where echeverias stretch.
Spine-tipped and genuinely dangerous at eye height. Dies after flowering, once, after decades.
The swollen caudex is a water store; a soft one means rot has already started. Drops all leaves in winter.
Neither a palm nor a cactus. Deciduous — bare in winter is the plant resting, not dying.
Do not water while a new pair of leaves is absorbing the old one. Watering then splits the plant.
Grows in winter and rests in summer — the opposite of most succulents. Summer leaf drop is normal.
Takes hard pruning and is often trained as bonsai. Edible, mildly sour — unlike the jade it resembles.
The red claw tips need direct sun. Loses leaves at the base if watered overhead.
Not a fern at all — it flowers and sets berries, and it has thorns on older stems.
Stores water in tuberous roots, so it forgives a missed week that would kill a true fern.
The one small fern that tolerates ordinary room humidity, though it still resents drying out fully.
Sheds far less than a Boston fern, which is usually why people buy it.
Grows from a furry surface rhizome — bury that and it rots. Sensitive to chlorine; use filtered water.
Wants genuinely humid air. In a dry room it browns at the edges within weeks whatever the watering.
Hardy outdoors to about -20°C. New fronds emerge copper and green up over a few weeks.
Faintly lemon-scented when brushed. The most compact of the Boston fern relatives.
Slow indoors. Leaf tips brown on every palm in dry air — trim following the natural edge, not straight across.
Tolerates lower light than any other palm sold indoors, and lives for decades in the same pot.
A cycad, not a palm. Every part is severely toxic to dogs and cats — keep it out of reach entirely.
Has spines at the frond base near the trunk. Wear gloves when cleaning out old fronds.
Clumping and thirsty — it grows beside streams in the wild and shows it the moment the pot dries.
Handles a dim corner better than areca and is far less prone to spider mite.
The hardest calathea sold. Tap water minerals brown the white sections within a month — use distilled.
Pink pinstripes fade with age on each leaf; that is normal, not a care failure.
Wavy leaf edges are the species, not dehydration. Judge thirst by the soil, not the leaf shape.
Folds up at night and reopens by morning. A plant that stays folded at midday is thirsty.
Thin papery leaves show every mistake. Keep it away from radiators and draughts both.
Stand the pot in rainwater or distilled. Tap water kills every carnivorous plant in this list within weeks.
Catches fungus gnats on its sticky leaves, which is why people keep it near other houseplants.
Wants cold roots and warm tops — it grows in mountain seeps. The hardest of the common carnivores.
Soak for 20 minutes, then shake it out and dry it upside down. Water left in the centre rots the crown.
Needs misting several times a week in a normal room; it has no roots and no reservoir.
Needs a cool, dry winter rest to set buds. Fed and watered all winter it grows leaves instead of flowers.
Pleated leaves mean it went dry too long — the fold is permanent on that leaf, so judge by new growth.
Wants more light than a phalaenopsis: leaves should be mid-green, not dark. Flowers last two to three weeks.
Needs a 10°C day-night swing in autumn to spike. Outdoors in early autumn is the usual trick.
Grown for the velvet leaves and their red veins; the flowers are small and white. Happy in a terrarium.
Water into the central cup and flush it monthly. Flowers once, then pups — the parent is finishing, not sick.
The centre turns red as it comes into flower. Same cup watering, same one-and-done life cycle.
The pink bract lasts months; the actual flowers are small and brief. Keep the cup topped up.
Needs six weeks cold and nearly dry in winter to flower. Resents being repotted and flowers better pot-bound.
Flowers from the stored bulb. To rebloom, feed the leaves all summer, then rest it dry and dark for eight weeks.
Wants a cool room, 12–16°C. Water from below only — the crown rots if water sits in it. Dormant in summer.
Furry leaves spot if splashed. Goes fully dormant after flowering; store the tuber dry and it returns.
Flowers for most of the year in a bright north window. Related to African violets and watered the same way.
Runs on stolons like a strawberry. Wants warmth — below 15°C it stops and rots at the crown.
Grows from scaly rhizomes and takes a dormant spell. Cut it back and keep it barely damp when it sulks.
Wants acidic soil, soft water and humidity, and drops buds if any one changes. The hardest plant on this list.
Needs about six weeks below 13°C in autumn to set buds. A warm room all winter means no flowers.
Each flower lasts one day. Bud drop after a move or a dry spell is the plant reacting, not a pest.
Flowers hardest when kept slightly dry and slightly hungry. Well-fed and well-watered it makes leaves only.
Needs six hours of direct sun to fruit indoors, and a citrus feed — yellow leaves are usually nitrogen, not water.
The most reliable indoor citrus. Fruit is edible but sour; it hangs on the tree for months.
Wants a bright cold winter, not a warm dark one. Indoors year-round it slowly thins and drops leaves.
Acidic soil and a cool spot. Buds form in late summer, so a dry August is what costs you spring flowers.
Sold in flower, then usually killed by a warm room. It wants 10–15°C and soil that never dries.
The red is bracts, triggered by 14 hours of true darkness nightly for eight weeks. Milky sap irritates skin.
Never cut the bare stalk a flower cluster came from — next year's flowers come from that same spur.
The one hoya that will not tolerate drying hard. Wants cool, humid air and fine bark, not compost.
Thick coin leaves store weeks of water. Splashed silver flecking is the plant, not a deficiency.
The crumpled leaves trap water and mealybugs equally. Check inside the folds when something looks off.
An epiphyte — it wants bark and air at the roots. In dense compost it rots from the base within a season.
Flowers on mature growth, so resist cutting it back hard. Leaf drop means cold, not thirst.
Wants the same care as a lipstick plant. Buds abort if it dries out while they are forming.
Brightest chartreuse in good light; in a dim spot it goes plain green and the stems stretch.
Needs real humidity or it drops everything and dies back to the tuber. Often returns in spring if kept barely damp.
Looks like ivy, drinks like a succulent. Watered like ivy it collapses.
Tolerates offices and dim corners. Mildews in stagnant air — give it a little movement.
Spider mite is the usual end of an indoor ivy. Cool and humid keeps them off better than any spray.
Deeply corrugated leaves. Water into the compost, not the crown, which rots readily.
Tiny and slow. Buried strands root where they touch, so it thickens if you tuck them back in.
Often mistaken for a pilea. Thicker, more succulent leaves and a longer safe gap between waterings.
Grows from a surface rhizome. Powdery mildew is the usual problem; airflow beats any treatment.
Goes dormant in autumn. Store the tuber dry and frost-free and it comes back bigger.
Neither strawberry nor begonia. Sends out runners with plantlets that root in any pot you place under them.
Curling leaves are the cultivar, not a problem. Same fluoride sensitivity as the plain spider plant.
Juvenile leaves are arrowhead-shaped and pink; on a pole it matures into large lobed green leaves.
The purple needs real sun. In shade it greens and the stems run. Cuttings root in water in under a week.
Fast and cheap to replace, which is the honest reason to buy it. Goes bald at the centre — restart it yearly.
Furry leaves mark if watered overhead, and the fuzz traps dust. Water at the soil line.
Only the French form has flavour, and it sets no seed — anything grown from seed is the tasteless Russian one.
Sweeter and less peppery than oregano, and far less hardy. Treat it as an annual outside zone 9.
Slow, long-lived, and happiest pot-bound. Scale insects on the leaf undersides are the usual problem.
Thirsty and frost-tender. A supermarket stalk stood in water roots in a fortnight and becomes a plant.
Bolts in heat and full sun. Sow it in succession in part shade and treat each sowing as six weeks of leaf.
Inhibits most neighbours — grow it on its own. Bolts to seed if it is checked by drought when young.
The classic bean herb. Annual, so let one plant set seed and it returns in the same bed.
Sweetest just before it flowers; pinch the buds out to keep the leaves worth picking.
Self-seeds enthusiastically. Pinch the flower spikes or the leaves go coarse and bitter.
A cat will flatten a young plant. Grow it caged or out of reach until it is established.
Pick the flowers every few days or it stops making them. Poor soil gives better scent than rich soil.
Needs warmth above 20°C to set fruit. Flea beetles shred the leaves of young plants — cover them early.
Cut the central head and it makes side shoots for weeks. Heat makes it bolt and go loose.
The fussiest brassica: any check in growth — drought, transplant shock, cold — gives a button head.
Heads split after heavy rain following a dry spell. Harvest before, or twist the plant to break some roots.
Needs a long season and firm soil. Sprouts that blow open usually mean loose planting, not bad seed.
Crops for months from one sowing if you take outer leaves and leave the centre alone.
Each seed is a cluster of several. Thin them or you get a knot of small roots instead of one good one.
Fast — six to eight weeks. Left longer they go woody and hot rather than larger and sweeter.
Earth up as the stems grow. Any tuber exposed to light goes green, and green potato is not edible.
Needs a long hot season. The ornamental trailing kinds sold for pots are the same species and do make tubers.
Hand-pollinate on cool mornings if the small fruit yellow and drop — that is a pollination failure, not disease.
Cure the fruit in warmth for a fortnight after cutting, and it keeps until spring.
Wind-pollinated, so plant it in a block rather than a row or the cobs come out half filled.
Stop watering as the fruit ripens — wet roots at the end give a watery, flavourless melon.
Ripe when the curly tendril nearest the fruit dries and the patch on the ground turns cream.
Drop the seedlings into deep dibbed holes and water them in without backfilling — that is what blanches the shank.
Plant in autumn; it needs a cold spell to split into cloves. Spring-planted garlic often makes one round bulb.
One set makes a cluster. Stop watering once the necks soften, then lift and dry them hard.
One of the few vegetables that genuinely wants constantly wet soil. Dry spells give stringy, bitter stalks.
Do not cut any spears for two years after planting. A bed left to establish then crops for twenty.
Pull the stalks, never cut them. The leaves are toxic — compost them, do not eat them.
Summer kinds fruit on last year's canes and autumn kinds on this year's. Pruning the wrong one costs a whole crop.
Needs acidic soil, pH 4.5–5.5, and rainwater. Tap water alone will slowly yellow it in a pot.
Fruits better with the roots restricted. A fig in open rich ground makes wood and very little fruit.
Needs several years and a lot of direct sun before it flowers indoors. Split leaves are normal, not damage.
Grows to the ceiling and does not branch. Buy it for the leaves; indoor flowers are rare.
Drinks and feeds more than anything else indoors. Each stem fruits once and is then replaced by a pup.
Leaf edges brown in dry air and scorch in direct sun. Fruits after three or four years in good conditions.
Fluoride and salts brown the tips like a spider plant. Filtered water fixes more than any change in feeding.
The standard dim-office plant, and deservedly so. Over-watering is the only reliable way to kill it.
Wants brighter light than other dracaenas to keep the yellow margins from fading out.
Grows from a rhizome and wants boggy soil while in leaf, then a dry rest after the foliage dies back.
Folds when touched and reopens in minutes. Short-lived — treat it as a one- or two-year plant and save seed.
Stand the pot in a saucer of water permanently. It is a marginal aquatic and cannot be over-watered.
Same standing-water treatment as papyrus. The one houseplant where a full saucer is correct.
Pinch the flower spikes off — flowering ends the leaf colour. Cuttings root in water in days.
Flowers best kept slightly dry and slightly pot-bound. Deadhead by snapping the whole stalk at the base.
Grown for the leaf scent rather than the small flowers. Takes hard pruning and roots from any cutting.
Wants cool shade, not sun. Pinch tips until midsummer for flowers all over rather than only at the ends.
The shade bedding plant. Downy mildew wipes out whole beds — rotate where you plant it each year.
Takes sun or shade, which is rare. One of the few bedding plants that does not need deadheading.
In containers it is a heavy feeder — flowering stops within weeks without regular liquid feed.
Planted among vegetables for a reason: the scent deters whitefly. Deadhead and it flowers until frost.
Do not feed it — rich soil gives leaves and no flowers. Leaves and flowers are edible and peppery.
Young heads track the sun; mature ones settle facing east. Stake tall kinds before they need it.
Water at the base. Wet foliage in still air gives powdery mildew every time.
Thrives on neglect and poor soil. Feed it and you get a tall leafy plant that flops and barely flowers.
Pick every few days. The moment it sets a seed pod the whole plant starts shutting down.
A cool-season plant. It flowers through frost and collapses in summer heat — that is its life span, not failure.
The orange beads last months in a cool room and drop fast in a warm one. Water from below.
Needs a bright cold winter to flower. Fast, shallow-rooted and easily blown over in a pot.
Cut it back hard every spring for the round juvenile leaves; left alone it makes long adult ones and a tree.
Clumping, so it does not run — the invasive reputation belongs to Phyllostachys, not this one.
